title: Robot API reference
text: Programs are the body of an async function: they run top to bottom, and every robot call must be awaited (`await robot.moveJ('P1')`). Units are millimeters and degrees. Poses are `{x, y, z, rx, ry, rz}` in the robot base frame, with orientation R = Rx(rx)·Ry(ry)·Rz(rz). A tool pointing straight down is `rx: 180, ry: 0`.

title: robot.moveJ(target, opts?)
text: Joint move. Every joint moves at once along the fastest path, so the tool does not follow a straight line. `target` is a target name (string) or a pose. For a taught target, the stored joint configuration is reused exactly. Use it for large moves between approach points. `opts.speed` is 1–100 percent (default 50).

title: robot.moveL(target, opts?)
text: Linear move. The tool travels in a straight line with its orientation interpolated. Use it for the last few centimeters of approach and retreat (pick, place, insert). It can fault with SINGULARITY when the path passes near a singular configuration, or with UNREACHABLE when part of the line leaves the workspace.

title: robot.moveJoints(jointsDeg, opts?)
text: Move to explicit joint angles, in degrees (millimeters for a prismatic joint). The array length must equal the number of joints.

title: robot.home(opts?)
text: Joint move to the arm's home configuration.

title: robot.getPose() / robot.getJoints()
text: Return the current tool pose, or the joint angles in degrees.

title: robot.wait(ms)
text: Wait in simulated time.

title: gripper.open() / gripper.close() / gripper.holding()
text: Closing takes 0.4 s. A part is picked up only if the tool center point (TCP, between the fingertips) is within about 15 mm of the part's vertical axis, sits between the bottom 10% and the top of the part, and the gripper is aligned with the part's up axis (pointing down onto it, within 15°). The part must also be narrower than the gripper stroke (60 mm). `holding()` returns the part id or null. Opening releases the part, which drops straight down onto whatever is below it.

title: io.get(name) / io.set(name, value) / io.waitFor(name, value, timeoutMs?)
text: Digital and text signals. Inputs come from sensors, e.g. `part_present` (true when a part waits at the end of the conveyor) and `part_color` ('red' | 'green' | 'blue' | 'none'). Outputs drive equipment, e.g. `conveyor_run`. `waitFor` blocks until the input equals the value. If `timeoutMs` is given and runs out, it faults with TIMEOUT.

title: targets.get(name) / targets.list()
text: Read target poses (a copy), or list every target name, taught and cell-defined.

title: offset(target, dx, dy, dz)
text: Returns a pose shifted in the base frame by dx, dy, dz millimeters. Use it for approach points (`offset('pick', 0, 0, 120)`) and grids (`offset('pallet.corner', col * 70, row * 70, layer * 50)`). It is synchronous, so don't await it.

title: log(...values)
text: Print to the Console tab.

title: sync()
text: Multi-arm tasks only. "Wait for each other": the arm stops here until every arm's program has reached its matching `sync()`. The 1st `sync()` in each program pairs with the 1st in every other program, the 2nd with the 2nd, and so on, so every program needs the same number of them, in the same order. Don't put `sync()` inside a loop or an if unless every arm runs it exactly as often. If an arm finishes while another is waiting, or the programs don't match, the run stops with SYNC_MISMATCH.

title: robot.moveTogether(target, opts?) / robot.follow()
text: Multi-arm tasks only. "Move together": one arm calls `robot.moveTogether(target)` and every other arm calls `robot.follow()` at the same point (it pairs up like `sync()`). The leading arm moves in a straight line to its own `target`; each following arm keeps exactly the distance and angle it had to the leader, so a part held by several arms is carried rigidly. Use it to lift and place a two-handed part. All arms start and stop together. Faults on any arm stop all of them.

title: Block reference
text: Programs start at the "When Run is pressed" block. Blocks that aren't attached below it are greyed out and ignored.

title: Motion
text:
- Go home (speed %): joint move to the home configuration.
- Move to [target] [joint move | straight line] speed %: a joint move is fastest; a straight line keeps the tool on a line, for approach and retreat. The target dropdown lists taught and cell targets, and "＋ Teach current pose…" teaches a new target directly from the dropdown.
- Move to [target] shifted by X Y Z mm: moves to a target offset in the base frame, for approach heights and grids. X, Y and Z accept numbers, variables and arithmetic blocks.

title: Gripper
text:
- Open gripper / Close gripper: a part between the fingers is picked up on close.
- If the gripper is holding a part … otherwise …

title: Signals
text:
- Wait until [input] is [value] (timeout s, 0 = forever): e.g. wait until part_present is true.
- If [input] is [value] … otherwise …: e.g. if part_color is red.
- Set [output] to [value]: e.g. set conveyor_run to false.
- sensor [input]: the current value, for use in comparisons.

title: Flow
text:
- Repeat N times; count with i from A to B (variable i); repeat while; if.
- Wait N seconds; Show message (prints to the Console); note (a comment, does nothing).

title: Together (multi-arm tasks)
text:
Each arm has its own column, with its own "When Run is pressed" block. All arms start together.
- Wait for each other: every arm waits here until all arms reach it. Dropping it in one arm's column adds a copy to every column, on the same row; moving or deleting one copy does the same to all of them. A tall copy shows time that arm spends waiting.
- Move together to [target] speed %: this arm leads a straight-line move; every other column gets a "Follow [arm]" copy, and those arms keep their distance, so a part they all hold moves with them. Drag a Follow copy to make that arm the leader.
- Together blocks go directly in an arm's column, never inside a loop or if (the editor refuses the drop), because every arm must reach them the same number of times.

title: Data and variables
text: Number, arithmetic, text and true/false blocks, plus variables (create in the Variables category).

title: Teaching targets
text: Jog the arm, or switch on Hand guide and drag the handle at the tool, then press Teach. That saves the current tool pose and joint configuration as a named target (P1, P2, …; double-click to rename). Cell targets such as `pick` or `bin.drop` are predefined by the scene and are read-only. Programs refer to targets by name.

title: Joint move vs linear move
text: A joint move (moveJ, "joint move" in blocks) is fast and robust but follows a curved path. A linear move (moveL, "straight line") keeps the tool on a straight line, which is needed for approach and retreat near parts and fixtures. The usual pattern is: moveJ to an approach point above the part, moveL down, close the gripper, moveL back up.

title: Faults (protective stops)
text:
Every move is checked before the robot moves. If a check fails, the robot does not move, the program stops, and the faulting line or block is highlighted.
- UNREACHABLE: the target, or part of the line, is outside the workspace. Move the target closer, raise it, or use a different orientation.
- JOINT_LIMIT: a joint would exceed its limit. Re-teach the target with a different arm configuration.
- SINGULARITY: a linear move passes through a singular configuration (e.g. wrist axes aligned), so a joint would flip. Use moveJ, or move through an intermediate point.
- COLLISION: the arm, gripper or held part would hit a fixture (table, conveyor, bin walls). Add an approach point higher up.
- INVALID_ARG: unknown target or signal name, or a bad value.
- TIMEOUT: an io.waitFor timed out.
- RUNAWAY: the program looped for 3 s of real time without commanding the robot. Add a wait or a motion inside the loop.
- USER_ERROR: a JavaScript error, such as a typo or an undefined variable.

title: Simulated time
text: Simulated time only advances while a robot command executes (moves, waits, gripper actions). The conveyor and sensors run on simulated time. The speed slider changes how fast the simulation plays, never the outcome.

title: Conveyors and sensors
text: Parts spawn at the start of the belt while `conveyor_run` is true and stop at the end sensor, where `part_present` becomes true. Always wait for `part_present` before picking. Parts arrive one by one; after you pick one, the next moves up to the sensor.

title: Grasping
text: Approach from straight above (tool pointing down, `rx: 180`), lower with a linear move so the TCP is around the middle of the part, then close. Picked parts follow the gripper exactly. On release, a part drops straight down onto the highest surface below it. Parts can be stacked; a part tilted more than 30° when released topples over.

title: Pouring (kitchen cell)
text: Containers have a fill level. Tilting a held container more than 90° from upright pours. Flow grows with tilt, reaching full rate at 120°. Liquid lands in a container if the lip is within 40 mm (horizontally) above it; otherwise it spills. With the tool pointing down (`rx: 180`), setting `rx: -70` tilts the container by 110° toward −y. Return containers upright.

title: Palletizing patterns
text: Use nested loops with offset(): `for (let row = 0; row < 2; row++) for (let col = 0; col < 2; col++) { ... offset('pallet.corner', col * pitch, row * pitch, layer * height) ... }`. Approach every slot from above with an offset in z.

title: Multi-arm tasks
text: Some tasks have two arms in one cell, for example a **Left arm** and a **Right arm**. Each arm runs its own program, and all programs start together when you press Run. In blocks mode the Program app shows one column per arm; in code mode it shows one JavaScript editor per arm. The pendant is wider on these tasks so the columns fit side by side.

title: Choosing an arm
text: Jog, Positions, hand guide and Teach act on one arm at a time. Pick it with the arm buttons at the top of the Jog and Positions apps, or click an arm in the 3D view. The readout at the bottom left of the cell view names the arm it shows.

title: Positions belong to an arm
text: Each arm has its own positions, measured from its own base, so a position taught with the Left arm only appears in the Left arm's dropdowns. Two arms can have positions with the same name that are different places. **Teach all arms at once** (Positions app, or Teach all arms on Jog) saves one name for every arm at its current pose, which is handy for Move together.

title: Wait for each other
text: The "Wait for each other" block (`sync()` in code) makes every arm wait until all of them arrive. Use it whenever one arm must finish something before the other starts, for example: the left arm puts a part on a pad and moves away, then the right arm picks it up. Without it both programs run at full speed independently. Copies appear in every arm's column on the same row, so blocks on the same row happen at the same moment.

title: Move together
text: "Move together to [target]" in one arm's column, with "Follow" in the others (`robot.moveTogether(target)` and `robot.follow()` in code), moves all arms at once. The leader goes in a straight line to its target; followers keep their distance and angle to it. Use it to carry a part with two grippers: close both grippers on it, Wait for each other, then Move together.

title: Two-handed parts and handovers
text:
A two-handed part (like a wide propeller) is too wide for one gripper. It only lifts when every arm holding it moves together; trying to lift it with one arm stops the program with NEEDS_TWO_HANDS. Opening one gripper while it's lifted drops it.
A handover is a re-grasp: arm A holds the part, arm B closes its gripper on another spot of the same part, then arm A opens. While both grippers hold an ordinary part, neither arm can move it alone (SHARED_GRASP), so add a Wait for each other after A lets go.

title: Multi-arm faults
text:
- ARM_COLLISION: two arms (or a part one of them holds) would hit each other. Every move is checked against what the other arms are doing at the same time, so the robots stop before anything moves. Add a Wait for each other so one arm leaves first, or change a position.
- SHARED_GRASP: several arms hold the same part and one tried to move alone. Use Move together, or open one gripper first.
- NEEDS_TWO_HANDS: one arm tried to lift a two-handed part.
- SYNC_MISMATCH: the programs' Together blocks don't pair up, for example one arm finished while another waits, or two arms both lead the same Move together.

title: Running and stepping
text: The Program app shows what each arm is doing: Moving, Waiting for others, or Finished. Each column highlights its own running block, and a block where an arm is waiting glows. Pause freezes every arm. Step runs one command on every arm that has one ready, then pauses again.

title: Teach pendant apps
text: The teach pendant is the tablet on the right. It shows one app at a time. Open apps from the Home screen's grid. The dock at the bottom (Home, Program, Jog, Positions) switches between the four most-used apps, and "Home" at the top left returns from any other app. Under the screen are the hardware run keys: Run, Pause/Resume, Step, and the red STOP button. The status light at the top right shows Ready, Running, Paused or Protective stop.

title: Home app
text: The Home screen shows the current task card (goals met, e.g. 2/4) and a grid of apps: Program, Jog, Positions, I/O, Log and Settings. Tap the task card to open the Task screen with the brief, the goal checklist (each goal ticks green when it passes) and optional hints. A red dot on the Log tile means a fault was logged.

title: Program app
text: Where you build the program. In blocks mode, drag blocks from the toolbox and snap them under "When Run is pressed"; they run top to bottom. The Blocks / JavaScript switch at the top shows the read-only JavaScript generated from your blocks. In code mode (Settings > Programming style) this app is a JavaScript editor. Your program is kept when you switch to other apps. While a program runs, the block that is executing lights up.

title: Jog app
text: Moves the robot by hand. Pick a mode: "Axes 1–3" and "Axes 4–6" turn individual joints; "Linear" moves the tool in X/Y/Z; "Reorient" rotates the tool (Rx/Ry/Rz) in place. In Linear and Reorient you can move in the Base frame (the cell's axes) or the Tool frame (the gripper's own axes). Drag the round joystick for smooth motion (further = faster); the vertical rocker beside it drives the third axis (e.g. Z or J3). Tap an arrow to step by the chosen "Arrow step" (0.1, 1 or 10 mm or degrees). The readouts show live joint angles or tool position, with a bar showing how close each joint is to its limit. Buttons: Hand guide (drag the green handle at the tool in the 3D view; Move or Rotate), Open/Close gripper, Go home, and Teach position (saves the current pose as P1, P2, …). Jogging is disabled while a program runs.

title: Positions app
text: Lists taught positions. "Teach new position here" saves the current tool pose. "Your positions" are the ones you taught: Go to moves the arm there, the target icon re-teaches it at the current pose, the pencil renames it, and the bin deletes it. "Cell positions" (such as pick, place, bin.drop) come with the scene and are read-only, but you can still Go to them. Each row shows the X, Y, Z position in mm. Programs refer to positions by name.

title: I/O app (inputs and outputs)
text:
The I/O app is a live, read-only monitor of the cell's digital signals. It updates several times a second, also while a program runs. Each row has an LED and an ON/OFF chip.
- Inputs · sensors: signals the cell sends to the robot. Example: part_present turns ON when a part reaches the end of the conveyor (a light-gate sensor) and OFF when the part is picked away.
- Outputs: signals the robot sends to the cell. Example: conveyor_run, when ON, keeps the conveyor belt moving and new parts arriving; when OFF, the belt stops. Some cells also have a general-purpose output such as light that your program can switch to signal its state.
You cannot click a signal to toggle it. Signals change only from the cell (sensors) or from your program: the "Wait until <input> is <value>" block / io.waitFor(name, value) pauses the program until an input has that value, the "Set <output> to <value>" block / io.set(name, value) switches an output, and io.get(name) reads a signal. Use the I/O app to check what your program will see, e.g. watch part_present go ON before the robot reaches for a part. Cells without a conveyor or sensors (such as the kitchen) have no signals, and the app says so.

title: Log app
text: Program messages and faults, each stamped with simulated time in seconds. Write your own messages with log(...) or the "Show message" block. Faults (protective stops) appear in red with the reason, e.g. UNREACHABLE or COLLISION.

title: Settings app
text: Toggles: Show positions in the cell (draws a small frame at every position), Sound effects, Background music (demo only) and Volume. In the demo you can also choose a different robot arm for the task and switch Programming style between Blocks and Code. "Take the tour" replays the guided tour.

title: Run keys and the 3D view
text: Run (or Ctrl/Cmd+Enter) starts the program. Pause halts it after the current command; Step then runs one robot command at a time; Resume continues. STOP (or Esc) ends the run. If a move fails a check, the robot stops before moving and the status shows Protective stop. In the 3D cell view: drag to orbit, scroll to zoom, use "Sim speed" to run the simulation faster or slower, "Reset" to put every part back where it started (after a fault the card also offers "Reset scene"), and the camera button to reset the view.

title: Two-arm tasks on the pendant
text: On tasks with several arms the pendant is wider. The Program app shows a column per arm and a status line (Moving, Waiting for others, Finished). Jog and Positions have arm buttons at the top to pick the arm you jog and teach, and the Positions app adds Teach all arms at once. The I/O app is shared: every arm's program sees the same signals. Settings hides the Robot arm choice, because the cell decides the arms.

title: AI partner window
text: The AI partner button in the pendant's status bar opens a floating chat window you can drag anywhere. In the demo you can pick the model at the top of the window. Depending on the mode it can answer questions, show pictures of blocks or short example clips, make a step-by-step plan, and propose program changes that you preview and then Accept or Reject. It never changes your program without your click.
